placement.position_note: PARTY-LINE FRONTAGE, DERIVED FROM THE COMMITTED PLAT (T-0078). This building does not stand centred on a lot at a typology setback: it stands ON the north face of blk_south_water_wells, the block's South Water Street frontage, whose line and bearing are read from the block boundary in data/traces/vectors/thompson_lots.json — the same committed geometry the lot grid and the corridor gate are derived from. Its front wall is 1.50 m back from that lot line, which is the closest line the plat module's own margin allows and is not a measurement of this frontage, and its east wall is fixed by 3.0 m west of carpenter_south_water_store, which stands proud of the platted line and so cannot share a wall with the row. The bearing is the face's own, so the front looks square at South Water Street. The run carries no lateral offset, because a shared party wall is one wall and cannot wander. WHAT IS INVENTED IS STILL EVERYTHING THAT MATTERS: that a building stood here at all, which building it was, and that these particular units stood shoulder to shoulder. What the 1834 South Water Street view supports is the TREATMENT — a continuous working row of party walls rather than detached cottages set back on grass. The treatment is what this placement takes from it, and a run standing on any other face of the town is borrowing it from that one street: the view draws a row, it does not place this row. Standing on a derived block face is not standing on a recovered lot, and the side lot lines this row crosses were always conjectural.

The dwelling's existence, position and footprint are unchanged and still conjectural, and nothing here claims he slept in it — only that the town's need for this trade is met by a man the papers name rather than by one this project invented. The invented name this record used to carry, and its name_basis block, are retired: an invented name is not kept beside a documented one. No figure is drawn (docs/LIBERTIES.md L1); the placement is L205. He is placed nowhere in particular by his own record, which is the condition of taking ANY roof of his trade — a man the papers put on a named street takes only a roof the plat stands on that street (T-0367), and one they place somewhere this scene cannot honour is refused outright. residents.research_note: RECONSTRUCTED HOUSEHOLD - fourth of 4 cooper households in this layer, in the north division. A TOWN PACKING THOUSANDS OF HOGS A SEASON NEEDS COOPERS, AND THIS DATASET HELD NONE. Andreas records that Clybourne packed some 250 head of cattle and about 2,000 hogs in the season of 1833, that George W. Dole packed a further 250 cattle and 1,000 hogs at the same place, and that the Newberry & Dole house on the South Branch packed 300 cattle and 1,400 hogs in 1834 (scan p. 1151). Packed provisions travel in barrels and barrels are made by coopers. The documented layer holds a packer, two slaughter-houses and not one cooper. Four cooper households are inferred against the schedule's six W3 cooper, wagon or wheelwright shops. METHOD: the count comes from the occupation census in data/reconstruction/1835_inferred_household_programme.json, which calibrates every trade against three things this project already holds - the 1835 town census (3,265 people, 398 dwellings), Andreas's roster of the fall of 1833 (about fifty named people, most with a trade, in a settlement of some 350), and the reconstruction specification's roof schedule, whose workshop and store family targets are treated as the ceiling on a trade rather than as its measure. Every count is stated NET of the documented layer: this dataset infers a tradesman only where it cannot name one. RETIRED AN INVENTED NAME (T-0264). This household was raised by the occupation census and named from the invented-name pools. The newspaper register matched it to J. Garland, a documented cooper the corpus names 1 time(s) and places nowhere in particular, and he now holds the roof. What changed is WHO: the argument for the household, its dwelling and its position are untouched and still the reconstruction's, and the person's grade is `inferred` — a real man with reconstructed details — rather than `attested`, which would claim the dwelling too. tools/replace_invented_residents.py derives this deal and prints every candidate it refused. frontage.why: T-0078, and the owner's standing ruling of 2026-08-18 with it: "there should be more and denser buildings. this is important." The reference he supplied for this reach — "South Water Street in 1834", the south bank of the Main Branch — shows a CONTINUOUS WORKING ROW: one-storey log and frame buildings shoulder to shoulder facing the river, the street between them and the grassy bank, two-storey frame stores anchoring its east end. This block's anonymous roofs stood seven metres back from that frontage, a full lot apart, each nudged off the line by its own lateral offset and — because the placement rule takes its bearing from the way into the lot — facing the block's interior rather than the river. That is the shape of a distribution across a block, not of a street. They now stand ON the frontage: the line, its bearing and the end they pack back from are read from the committed block boundary in data/traces/vectors/thompson_lots.json, and this recipe authors no coordinate for any of them. The 1.5 m setback is not a measurement of this frontage — it is the closest line the plat module's own lot margin allows, adopted so the street wall is one wall. NO ROOF IS ADDED: the run carries exactly the roofs the schedule dealt this block's frontage lots, with every id, family and dimension the one it already had. What the view drives is the treatment — a row on its line, facing the water — never a coordinate, and the side lot lines the row crosses between its own units were conjectural in every record this generator has ever written.
